records.sourceFile: Nutrient intake, meal timing and sleep in elite male Australian football players.pdf

paper.citation: Falkenberg E, Aisbett B, Lastella M, Roberts S, Condo D. Nutrient intake, meal timing and sleep in elite male Australian football players. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2020.
paper.abstract: This cohort study tracked sleep with actigraphy and sleep diaries, and dietary intake with photo food diaries, in 36 elite male Australian Football League players across 10 pre-season days. Higher total daily protein intake was associated with more wake after sleep onset and lower sleep efficiency, and higher evening sugar intake was associated with less total sleep time and less wake after sleep onset. A longer gap between the evening meal and bedtime was associated with less total sleep time.
paper.tldr: In elite Australian football players, evening sugar intake and the time gap between the last meal and bedtime were the dietary factors most linked to sleep. These are observational associations, not tested dietary changes.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort study of 36 male players from one professional club over 10 consecutive pre-season days. Sleep was measured with wrist actigraphy (medium threshold) and sleep diaries, and food intake with the MealLogger photo app and FoodWorks analysis; generalised linear mixed models adjusted for training load, previous-night sleep, travel, chronotype, alcohol, caffeine, age and body mass.
paper.findings: Higher total daily protein (g/kg) was linked to more wake after sleep onset (+4.0 min, P = 0.013) and lower sleep efficiency (-0.7%, P = 0.006). Higher evening sugar (g/kg) was linked to less total sleep time (-5.1 min, P = 0.027), less wake after sleep onset (-1.0 min, P = 0.005) and slightly higher sleep efficiency (+0.2%, P = 0.021), and higher evening energy was linked to longer sleep onset latency (+5.0 min per MJ, P = 0.011). Each extra hour between the main evening meal and bedtime was linked to 8.1 min less total sleep time (P = 0.042) and 2.3 min less wake after sleep onset (P = 0.015).
paper.limitations: The study is observational, with a single club and 36 players, and sleep and food intake were estimated by actigraphy, diaries and a photo app that has not been validated against weighed food records. The abstract attributes the sleep-onset-latency association to total daily energy intake, but Table 1 shows no such association (0.7 min, P = 0.116); the association is for evening energy intake (5.0 min, P = 0.011, Table 2). For evening protein (g/kg) and sleep onset latency, the abstract gives P = 0.02 and the Discussion a 4-min decrease, while Table 2 and the Results give -2.2 min (P = 0.016).
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners could raise evening sugar intake and the timing of the last meal with players who sleep poorly, since these were the factors most linked to sleep in this group. The authors' advice to take whey protein before bed is not supported by these data, because protein type was not analysed and no intervention was tested. Eating closer to bedtime was linked to longer sleep time but more wake time after sleep onset, so staff should not assume that a later meal is simply better or worse for sleep.
paper.athleteDev: In elite male Australian football players, higher evening sugar intake and a longer gap between the evening meal and bedtime were linked to less total sleep, and higher total daily protein was linked to more wake time after sleep onset. These findings suggest topics to review with players, but they do not show that changing these intakes would improve sleep or performance.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It did not study injured players, and it did not measure sleep or nutrition during rehabilitation, return-to-play clearance or re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Nutrition for Travel- from Jetlag to Catering.pdf

paper.citation: Halson SL, Burke LM, Pearce J. Nutrition for Travel- from Jetlag to Catering. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018.
paper.abstract: This scholarly review covers the travel challenges of high-performance athletes, mainly track and field athletes, including jetlag, fatigue and gastrointestinal comfort, travel hygiene and illness, and catering in unfamiliar environments. It discusses melatonin, caffeine and meal timing and composition for jetlag, and it sets out shared responsibilities among athletes, team management and caterers for food and water safety and eating behaviour.
paper.tldr: Traveling athletes face jetlag, travel fatigue, illness and catering problems that planning can reduce. The evidence for melatonin, caffeine and meal timing against jetlag is limited, and the review treats food safety and eating behaviour as shared responsibilities.
paper.methods: Scholarly narrative review. The authors cover jetlag, travel fatigue and eating en route, travel hygiene and catering, and provide checklists for caterers, teams and athletes. No systematic search or study-selection method is described.
paper.findings: Melatonin shifts the body clock in a direction that depends on the timing of intake, and a cited systematic review found it reduced subjective jetlag compared with placebo. A cited study found 300 mg of slow-release caffeine at 08:00 destination time for 5 days resynchronised faster than placebo. The review reports that illness rose two- to threefold with travel across more than five hours' time difference, citing earlier work.
paper.limitations: The review has no described search or appraisal method, so its selection of evidence cannot be checked. The authors note that meal composition and timing effects on jetlag have not been well studied in athletes, and that melatonin product content varied from 18% to 478% of the labelled amount in one cited survey.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan meals, snacks and fluids around the travel itinerary, and for athletes prone to motion sickness the review lists avoiding large meals, caffeine and alcohol before and during travel. Agree team food and hygiene protocols before departure and check destination food and water safety. Check supplements such as melatonin for content and banned substances before use, because the review reports that product content varies.
paper.athleteDev: For traveling track and field athletes, planned meal timing, food access and fluid intake before and during travel are presented as ways to limit jetlag and fatigue effects on performance. The review's evidence for melatonin, caffeine and meal timing against jetlag is limited, so these tools should be trialled rather than assumed to work.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It covers travel nutrition, illness prevention and catering for traveling athletes and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play.

records.sourceFile: Nutrition for optimising immune function and recovery from injury in sports.pdf

paper.citation: Rotovnik Kozjek N, Tonin G, Gleeson M. Nutrition for optimising immune function and recovery from injury in sports. Clinical Nutrition ESPEN. 2025;66:101-114.
paper.abstract: This educational narrative review describes how nutrition relates to immune function, sports injury, detraining and rehabilitation in athletes. It sets out nutritional targets for energy, protein, carbohydrate, fat and micronutrients, and tabulates supplement recommendations. The authors conclude that a quality whole-food diet comes first and that supplements are mainly indicated for documented deficiencies.
paper.tldr: Injured or training athletes need adequate energy, protein and carbohydrate from quality whole foods, and supplements are generally limited to documented deficiencies such as vitamin D. The supplement tables give specific doses, but many carry limited or no clear evidence.
paper.methods: Educational narrative review with learning objectives, written by three authors. It covers injury terminology and stages, detraining, immunometabolism, immunodepression and moderating factors, and nutritional targets, drawing on cited literature. No search strategy or study-selection method is described.
paper.findings: The review notes that immobilisation causes muscle mass loss of about 0.5-0.6% per day. It gives post-injury targets of 1.6-2.5 g/kg/day protein and carbohydrate of 3-5 g/kg/day, and says low energy availability (<30 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day) should be avoided. Supplement tables rate glutamine as having no clear benefit for infection incidence, and report that vitamin C at 0.25-1.0 g/day may reduce the incidence, duration and severity of common colds in athletes.
paper.limitations: The review has no described search or appraisal method, so the evidence base and the strength of each recommendation cannot be checked. Several recommendations are extrapolated from immobilisation, non-athlete or small studies, and the authors state that evidence for immune-supporting supplements is limited.
paper.practicalImplications: For injured athletes, the review recommends individually adjusted energy and protein intake, with whole-food sources spread across the day, before supplements are considered. It recommends a seasonal check of serum vitamin D as part of routine medical examination, with treatment of deficiency, and says iron deficiency should be treated only under medical supervision. Antioxidant supplements are not recommended in the review, which cites evidence that high vitamin C plus vitamin E intake can impair training adaptation, and third-party testing is advised for any supplement.
paper.athleteDev: The review's performance-related content is limited to energy availability, and to protein and carbohydrate targets for training and immune health. It frames a quality diet as the first line of immune support, and it does not test performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review gives nutrition targets during immobilisation and rehabilitation and states that nutritional support can aid the return to activity. It did not study return-to-sport outcomes and sets no return-to-play criteria, so it cannot be used to decide whether an athlete is ready to return.

records.sourceFile: Nutritional approaches applied to recovery of skeletal muscle injury immobilization - A review of nutrition aid for sport trauma.pdf

paper.citation: Rocha-Rodrigues S, Leão C, Marinho M, Afonso J. Nutritional approaches applied to recovery of skeletal muscle injury immobilization: a review of nutrition aid for sport trauma. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2024 Sep 17.
paper.abstract: The authors review current evidence on nutritional approaches to skeletal muscle injury recovery in athletes, covering energy intake, proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins and omega-3 fatty acids. They conclude that evidence from injured athletes is scarce, so specific guidelines cannot yet be established.
paper.tldr: Evidence on nutrition for recovering from a muscle injury in athletes is thin. Most of it comes from healthy people with immobilization or induced soreness, so it cannot yet support specific guidelines for injured athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature on nutrition and skeletal muscle injury recovery. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: The authors report that energy needs after injury are variable and recommend monitoring body fat percentage rather than relying on energy expenditure estimates. Creatine results during immobilization in healthy young people were mixed: one small crossover study (n=7, arm cast) and one trial (n=22, leg immobilization) reported preserved or restored muscle mass, while another trial (n=30, leg immobilization) found no effect on muscle mass or strength. A 5-day hydrolysed whey study in young professional soccer players (n=24) reported lower creatine kinase (-42%) and lactate dehydrogenase (-30%) than maltodextrin, and the authors describe evidence for vitamin C, omega-3 and carbohydrate in injured athletes as absent or indirect.
paper.limitations: Most cited data come from healthy or non-injured people, soreness models, or two case studies of soccer players after anterior cruciate ligament injury. No specific guidelines for injured athletes could be formed, and the review does not describe how studies were selected.
paper.practicalImplications: Energy and protein intake during injury recovery should be individualized by the athlete's immobilization level, activity and body composition. Staff should not treat the reviewed supplement findings as an established protocol for injured athletes.
paper.athleteDev: The review offers no performance-enhancement recommendation. Its supplement findings come from healthy or non-injured people.
paper.rtp: Cannot be used to set a nutrition protocol or a return-to-play timeline for injured athletes. The authors state that specific guidelines for injured athletes cannot yet be established.

records.sourceFile: Nutritional interventions for reducing the signs and symptoms of exercise-induced muscle damage and accelerate recovery in athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Bongiovanni T, Genovesi F, Nemmer M, Carling C, Alberti G, Howatson G. Nutritional interventions for reducing the signs and symptoms of exercise-induced muscle damage and accelerate recovery in athletes: current knowledge, practical application and future perspectives. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2020.
paper.abstract: The authors review nutritional strategies for the signs and symptoms of exercise-induced muscle damage and group them by level of supporting evidence. They conclude that the evidence is mixed and suggest a periodised approach to supplementation until more is known about effects on adaptation.
paper.tldr: The authors place vitamin D, omega-3, creatine, tart cherry, beetroot and pomegranate in their best-researched group, but they say this does not mean the supplements are clearly effective, and for vitamin D they find no clear recovery benefit. Where these are used, the authors suggest periodising them around high-stress phases rather than using them all the time.
paper.methods: Invited review. The authors report searching PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus and Web of Science using combinations of EIMD and nutrition terms. No study count, inclusion criteria or risk-of-bias method is reported.
paper.findings: The good-evidence group is defined by the amount of research, and results within it are mixed. For vitamin D, one trial in 20 deficient, moderately active men found better recovery of muscle function after 6 weeks of 4000 IU/day, while other trials found no effect, and the authors conclude there is no clear benefit for recovery after damaging exercise. Creatine trials show both lower creatine kinase (for instance, 84% lower in one 5-day study of 14 untrained men) and no effect (for instance, 40 g loading then 10 g daily); vitamins C and E show limited ability to reduce EIMD signs, and a cited Cochrane review rates antioxidant evidence for soreness as moderate to low quality.
paper.limitations: Study designs, doses, timing and outcome measures vary widely, and many trials use untrained or recreationally active participants rather than well-trained athletes. The tiering is internally inconsistent for vitamin D, which is placed in the good-evidence group and Table 1 with a 2000 to 4000 IU daily dose although the text finds no clear recovery benefit. The authors also note that cross-over designs can mask effects through the contralateral repeated bout effect and that most redox measures are mechanistically limited.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest a regular, varied diet without added supplements during preseason adaptation phases, and carefully planned interventions when fast recovery is the priority, such as congested fixture schedules. Vitamin D should be used to maintain sufficient status rather than as a recovery aid, since the review finds no clear recovery benefit.
paper.athleteDev: The authors raise a theoretical concern that antioxidant or anti-inflammatory supplements could blunt training adaptation, while stating there is no evidence yet that these interventions do so; this is the basis for their periodised approach. The review does not show that any intervention improves performance or adaptation.
paper.rtp: The review concerns recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage, not injury. It cannot be used to set a return-to-play nutrition plan after a musculoskeletal injury.

records.sourceFile: Nutritional priorities, practices and preferences of athletes and active individuals in the context of new product development in the sports nutrition sector.pdf

paper.citation: Carey CC, Doyle L, Lucey A. Nutritional priorities, practices and preferences of athletes and active individuals in the context of new product development in the sports nutrition sector. Front Sports Act Living. 2023;5:1088979.
paper.abstract: The authors surveyed athletes and active individuals on their nutrition priorities, supplement and functional food use, and preferred product formats. They conclude that a food-first approach and evidence-based functional foods, focused on recovery, endurance and strength, should guide new sports nutrition products.
paper.tldr: Athletes in this Irish survey most wanted products that support muscle recovery and rated nutritional quality as the top purchase factor. Whole-food formats were the most preferred, though the survey measured preferences rather than product effects.
paper.methods: Online Qualtrics survey of 34 questions, developed from a literature review, two focus groups and a review of products on the Irish and online markets. Recruitment used social media, university email lists and clubs, and analyses were descriptive with Mann-Whitney U tests by gender, competition level and weekly activity time.
paper.findings: Enhanced muscular recovery was the top product claim (first choice 25%, n=101; top three 73%, n=295), ahead of improved endurance (top three 58%) and improved strength and power (57%). Nutritional profile was rated the most important purchase feature (3.37 ± 0.65 out of 4), ahead of taste (3.15 ± 0.80) and ease of access (3.09 ± 0.72). Fifty-eight percent reported taking supplements, 43% used bioactive functional foods, and whole-food products received the most first-choice rankings for both recovery (186) and performance (180) products.
paper.limitations: Recruitment was by convenience sampling in Ireland, the focus groups used to build the questionnaire did not reach saturation, and no health, performance or efficacy outcome was measured. The authors state that rank-order questions could not be compared statistically across gender or competition level; only the 1 to 4 rating questions were tested with Mann-Whitney U, so the discussion's claim that gender influenced the 'rank importance' of product features refers to ratings, not rankings. Some figures differ between text and tables, for example 202 top-three rankings for smoothie or juice in the results text versus 220 in Table 4, and 87% rating scientific proof at least 3 of 4 versus 86% in Table 3.
paper.practicalImplications: Most respondents who changed their recovery routine used stretching (n = 230) and foam rolling (n = 166), which the authors note have little effect on muscle damage recovery, while only 4% used dietary nitrate and 6% polyphenol foods. This points to an education gap staff can address, and to whole-food formats as the options athletes say they prefer.
paper.athleteDev: The survey covers performance-related product priorities, including endurance and strength claims, but it does not show that any product improves performance. Its findings describe preferences, not effects.
paper.rtp: The survey does not address injury or return to sport. It cannot be used to choose a recovery product or plan for an injured athlete returning to training.

records.sourceFile: Nutritional strategies to improve post-exercise recovery and subsequent exercise performance - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Naderi A, Rothschild JA, Santos HO, Hamidvand A, Koozehchian MS, Ghazzagh A, et al. Nutritional Strategies to Improve Post-exercise Recovery and Subsequent Exercise Performance: A Narrative Review. Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of nutritional strategies used to speed recovery and improve performance when athletes face short gaps between exercise bouts. It covers carbohydrate type and timing, protein, carbohydrate-protein co-ingestion, fluids and electrolytes, sodium bicarbonate, creatine, caffeine, fats and micronutrients.
paper.tldr: For the first 4 h after exercise, carbohydrate at about 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h, preferably with glucose and fructose in a 2:1 ratio, is the core recovery strategy. Protein, creatine, caffeine and sodium bicarbonate can help in some settings, but their performance effects are inconsistent.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar using keyword and Boolean combinations, then graded each strategy as strong, moderate or limited evidence. The paper does not report study counts, inclusion criteria or a formal quality appraisal.
paper.findings: Carbohydrate at 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h is recommended for the first 4 h, and glucose-fructose co-ingestion is preferred for gastrointestinal comfort and liver glycogen replenishment. The authors conclude that adding protein to carbohydrate during recovery shorter than 24 h likely has a small positive effect on performance (0.6 to 1.6%), although for glycogen resynthesis the benefit appears only when carbohydrate intake is suboptimal. Sodium bicarbonate may improve subsequent exercise when recovery is about 30 to 90 min, and creatine and caffeine can increase glycogen storage in some studies, though performance results are mixed. Fats have no clear effect on subsequent performance, and micronutrients reduce muscle damage without a clear performance benefit.
paper.limitations: The authors note a sex bias toward male participants, variable exercise protocols, and individual differences by training status and genetics. Several supplement effects are not additive, and the review does not describe a systematic search protocol or study quality appraisal.
paper.practicalImplications: When the next bout is less than 4 h away, athletes can take 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h of carbohydrate in small, frequent doses, preferably glucose-fructose at a 2:1 ratio. Adding 20 to 40 g of protein is reasonable when there is time for digestion. Caffeine or sodium bicarbonate can be considered for specific schedules, with attention to gastrointestinal discomfort and sleep disruption.
paper.athleteDev: Use 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h of carbohydrate in the first 4 h after training when the next session is less than 24 h away, with 20 to 40 g of protein added. Caffeine or sodium bicarbonate may suit athletes with multiple sessions in one day, but the review does not support them as a routine add-on.
paper.rtp: The review covers recovery between training or competition bouts within 24 h. It does not study injury or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Muscle Strength-Current State of Knowledge and Future Perspectives.pdf

paper.citation: Tomczyk M. Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Muscle Strength: Current State of Knowledge and Future Perspectives. Nutrients. 2024;16:4075.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of the effects of EPA and DHA supplementation on muscle strength in healthy adults and older adults, with a summary of trials and of the limitations that prevent firm conclusions. It also covers the proposed neuromuscular and inflammation-related mechanisms and supplement safety.
paper.tldr: Omega-3 (EPA and DHA) supplementation may produce a small strength gain in healthy and older adults, but the trials are few and inconsistent and most were not in athletes. It is not a proven strength strategy for athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal. Trials are summarized in a table by population, supplement dose, duration and outcome, and meta-analyses are described from the published literature.
paper.findings: Three of six adult trials reported higher strength with omega-3 than placebo (Heileson 2023 in bench press and squat 1RM, Philpott 2019 in leg extension 1RM, Crestani 2017 in knee extension 1RM). In the two athlete trials, Lewis 2015 (30 male athletes) found an unclear effect on quadriceps MVC force with higher vastus lateralis EMG, and Gravina 2017 (soccer players) found no strength difference; Lewis 2017 in active men also found no difference. Among older adults, Xu 2022 (187 participants, 6 months) reported higher grip strength and better Timed Up and Go times than placebo, while Krzymińska-Siemaszko 2015 (53 participants, 12 weeks) found no difference. Cited meta-analyses describe a very small but significant strength effect with low certainty (14 studies), and a network meta-analysis found the highest efficacy above 2.5 g/day.
paper.limitations: The author notes that many trials did not control training or diet, and that dose and duration affect how much omega-3 reaches tissues. The review does not describe how studies were selected. Adverse effects include a higher atrial fibrillation risk in some meta-analyses at high doses, and fishy aftertaste or burping.
paper.practicalImplications: Omega-3 supplementation is unlikely to produce more than a small strength gain, and the trials are small and mixed. If it is used, plan for a long enough period at a standardized dose, since the review cites about 12 weeks at 1000 to 1500 mg/day EPA and DHA to reach an omega-3 index of 8% (Dempsey et al., as cited). The author advises considering atrial fibrillation risk before starting, particularly at high doses or in high-risk individuals.
paper.athleteDev: The strength evidence comes mostly from recreationally trained and older adults, and the two athlete trials in the review found no clear strength gain. If omega-3 is trialled alongside resistance training, expect at most a small effect, track strength and tolerance, and do not treat it as a substitute for training or basic nutrition.
paper.rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes and cannot guide return-to-play decisions. Its injury remarks refer to general links between strength and injury rates from other studies.

records.sourceFile: Performance Enhancing Supplements and Cardiovascular Health.pdf

paper.citation: Singh M, Givens M, Singh T, Rao P. Performance Enhancing Supplements and Cardiovascular Health. Current Treatment Options in Cardiovascular Medicine. 2025;27:29.
paper.abstract: This narrative review covers performance enhancing supplements used by recreational athletes, including anabolic-androgenic steroids, testosterone and hormone therapy, caffeine and pre-workout products, and creatine. It summarizes mechanisms, reported benefits and cardiovascular risks, and proposes a risk-stratified approach based on education, screening and shared decision-making.
paper.tldr: The review links anabolic-androgenic steroid misuse to serious cardiovascular and metabolic harm. It describes low to moderate caffeine and creatine intake as carrying minimal cardiovascular risk in healthy athletes, and notes that the long-term effects of creatine still need study.
paper.methods: Narrative review with an opinion statement, drawing on prior trials, registry studies, meta-analyses and reviews. No search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal is described.
paper.findings: In 100 men on an AAS cycle, systolic and diastolic blood pressure rose by 6.87 and 3.17 mmHg, and LDL cholesterol rose by 0.45 mmol/L; many of these changes reversed after cessation. In the TRAVERSE trial, testosterone was noninferior to placebo for major adverse cardiac events but increased pulmonary embolism, acute kidney injury and non-fatal arrhythmias. Creatine at 10 g/day in healthy athletes did not alter creatine clearance or glomerular filtration rate over 10 months to 5 years, and the review states that caffeine above about 6 to 9 mg/kg may add little performance benefit while posing serious cardiovascular risk.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search, selection or risk-of-bias method. The registry estimate is subject to confounding, and the TRAVERSE trial had low adherence (39% completed the full study drug duration), which the review says biases results toward the null. The creatine safety data are short- to medium-term, and the authors call for longer prospective trials.
paper.practicalImplications: The review recommends regular checks of hormone levels, hematocrit, lipids, blood pressure and echocardiography for people using AAS. It advises low to moderate caffeine use, notes that many pre-workout products contain 200 mg or more per serving, and says excessive stimulant use warrants screening for comorbidities, genetic heart disease and symptoms. Creatine at about 5 g/day is described as largely safe, with weight gain and fluid retention to consider in people with hypertension or left ventricular dysfunction.
paper.athleteDev: The review describes creatine as improving high-intensity efforts under 30 seconds and supporting strength and power. Caffeine may improve endurance at low to moderate doses, but the benefit is not consistent, and high doses add little.
paper.rtp: This review does not address return to sport after injury, so it cannot set return-to-play timelines or medical clearance. Cardiovascular screening is relevant for athletes who use these supplements, but the review does not define clearance criteria.

paper.citation: Jeukendrup AE. Periodized Nutrition for Athletes. Sports Med. 2017;47(Suppl 1):S51-S63.
paper.abstract: Narrative review defining periodized nutrition (nutritional training) and summarising methods that manipulate carbohydrate availability, gut training, hydration and supplements to shape training adaptation. The author concludes that the methods differ in evidence strength and that most have little performance evidence so far.
paper.tldr: Nutrition can be timed and planned around training to shape adaptation, but most of these methods have little performance evidence yet. Choose methods to fit the goal, such as gut training for race fuelling, and treat the others as untested for performance.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy. The author defines periodized nutrition, then categorises methods in a table covering train low, train high, training the gut, training dehydrated and supplements, drawing on earlier reviews and selected primary studies.
paper.findings: Train-low methods such as twice-daily training, fasted training and sleep low have generally changed signalling and oxidative markers, but few have shown performance benefit; two cycling studies of twice-daily training found no performance difference after 3 weeks. In the only sleep-low study with a performance outcome, 10 km running improved within the sleep-low group (n=11) but not the control group (n=10), and in a 3-week study of elite endurance athletes the ketogenic diet group did not improve high-intensity performance (-1.6%) while high-carbohydrate (6.6%) and mixed (5.5%) groups did. The author also reports that caffeine and sodium bicarbonate improve performance within the durations studied and that high-dose antioxidants may blunt training adaptation.
paper.limitations: The review is selective and gives no search, quality appraisal or grading of evidence. Several examples are small early studies in untrained or recreational participants, the sleep-low evidence rests on two studies and the dehydrated-training evidence on one study of 10 recreationally active people. The article was published in a supplement supported by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (a division of PepsiCo), and the author received an honorarium from GSSI for the meeting and for writing the manuscript.
paper.practicalImplications: Match nutrition methods to the goal: gut training or race-nutrition practice fits endurance athletes with gastrointestinal problems, and caffeine (studied mostly in exercise of about 1 hour) or sodium bicarbonate (about 1 to 10 minutes) fit efforts of those durations. Treat train-low and dehydrated training as unproven for performance, note that the ketogenic diet studies cited showed no performance benefit, and avoid high-dose antioxidants if the goal is training adaptation.
paper.athleteDev: The review frames nutrition as a planned part of training, but finds few performance benefits so far for train-low, sleep-low or ketogenic approaches. It gives no clear guidance yet on fasted or dehydrated training.
paper.rtp: The review does not discuss injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform clinical recovery decisions after injury.

records.sourceFile: Personalized fluid and fuel intake for performance optimization in the heat.pdf

paper.citation: Cheuvront SN, Kenefick RW. Personalized fluid and fuel intake for performance optimization in the heat. J Sci Med Sport. 2021.
paper.abstract: Review of how individual sweat rate, thirst and sports-drink fuel targets interact during prolonged exercise in the heat. Using modelled sweat losses for 50 and 90 kg runners, the authors show that drinking to match sweat loss and meeting carbohydrate targets with one sports drink often cannot both be achieved.
paper.tldr: In the heat, drinking enough to limit dehydration and meeting carbohydrate targets from one sports drink often conflict. For longer runs the authors suggest food or more concentrated fuel, and a fluid plan based on individual sweat rate.
paper.methods: Narrative review with worked calculations. Evaporative heat balance and energy-cost equations estimate sweat rates for 50 and 90 kg runners at 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 L/h over 1, 2 and 4 hours, and the drinking rates needed to hold dehydration at or below 2% of body mass. Fuel targets are 30, 60 and 90 g/h carbohydrate, and thirst-based intake is modelled at 50% of sweat loss.
paper.findings: With no drinking, the modelled runners reach more than 2% dehydration in 11 of 18 scenarios, and drinking a typical sports drink (about 60 g carbohydrate per litre) to meet fluid needs would rarely meet fuel targets. Meeting the 90 g/h fuel target over 4 hours from sports drink alone would require substantial over-drinking. A modelled drink-to-thirst strategy (50% replacement) gave too much or too little fluid in 14 of 18 cases and missed fluid or fuel needs in 28 of 36, but never over-drank relative to sweat rate.
paper.limitations: This is a model with no participants and no measured sweat losses. Its results depend on the assumed 2% threshold, the 50% thirst replacement and the chosen sweat rates. The authors note that 50% is at the high end of reported thirst-driven intake, with others reporting around 20%, so thirst-based results may differ. The source is an accepted manuscript before copyediting, and the authors note that production errors may be found.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes running long events in the heat need a fluid and fuel plan tested in training, because one sports drink may not meet both needs. Knowing individual sweat rate helps set drinking volumes, and for exercise of about 2 hours or more the authors suggest food or concentrated carbohydrate sources, tested for tolerance, to meet fuel needs without over-drinking.
paper.athleteDev: For performance in the heat, the review suggests planning fluid and carbohydrate targets together, using individual sweat-rate estimates and gels or food for longer efforts. The modelled figures are not tested in athletes, so they guide planning rather than set targets.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address return to sport, heat illness after injury or rehabilitation. Its dehydration threshold concerns exercise performance in healthy runners, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.
